newsitem.title: USA: FCC approves Bell Atlantic-Nynex merger.
newsitem.headline: FCC approves Bell Atlantic-Nynex merger.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission Thursday approved the $25 billion merger of Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex Corp., sweeping away the last hurdle to creation of the nation's second biggest telephone company.
The FCC, as expected, attached several conditions to the deal, which will form the nation's largest local carrier and the No. 2 phone company after long-distance giant AT&T Corp.

The conditions are meant to ensure the two regional Bell phone companies open their 13-state market in the Northeast to rivals wanting to offer local service. The carriers agreed to them last month, paving the way for FCC clearance.
The Justice Department approved the transaction in April.

The deal was announced in April 1996. The new Bell Atlantic will serve an area stretching from Maine to Virginia with 39 million phone lines and will rank 23rd on Fortune magazine's list of the nation's 500 largest corporations.
The companies were expected to complete the deal shortly.

The new company will have more than 140,000 employees offering business and residential customers local, wireless and Internet services. The new company, which will have $50 billion in assets, is expected soon to seek approval to offer long-distance calling to its customers.
"That's the next move. They've been focused on having to get the merger approved," said Scott Cleland of Legg Mason Precursor Group, research arm of the Baltimore brokerage.
It is the second merger of regional Bells since the 1996 telecommunications law. SBC Communications Inc. and Pacific Telesis Group completed a $16.5 billion merger on April 1.

As a result of the FCC conditions, Bell Atlantic and NYNEX promised to create a uniform electronic system through which rivals can order services and handle installation, billing and other customer-service requirements without delays.
They agreed to offer smaller local phone rivals flexible payment plans for access to the local Bell phone network. That way, small companies are not hit with big up-front payments.
The two companies also agreed to charge new rivals prices based on "forward-looking" costs, rather than "embedded" costs that aim to recoup the cost of previously installed equipment.

And the companies agreed to disclose to the FCC data about their service and the quality of their phone network. Rivals could complain directly to the FCC if they feel that the new Bell Atlantic was not living up to the agreement.
